## Q1
How many comparisons are required in the worst case to find the second smallest element of a list of n elements?

## Q1 - Options
(A) n + ⌈log n⌉ − 1
(B) n + ⌈log n⌉
(C) ⌈log n⌉
(D) n + ⌈log n⌉ − 2

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q15

Finding the second smallest efficiently uses a tournament (knockout) method. Comparing elements in a single-elimination tournament to find the minimum takes n − 1 comparisons, and during that tournament the eventual minimum is directly compared against exactly ⌈log₂ n⌉ other elements, one at each round it wins.

The second-smallest element must be among those ⌈log₂ n⌉ elements that lost directly to the minimum, so finding the smallest among that shortlist takes ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 1 further comparisons.

(n − 1) + (⌈log₂ n⌉ − 1) = n + ⌈log n⌉ − 2, which is the worst-case comparison count.

## Q3
Match List I with List II on algorithm running times.

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Parallel FFT | I. Θ(n²) |
| B. Iterative FFT | II. Θ(n) |
| C. Evaluation of polynomial at n points by Horner method | III. Θ(lg n) |
| D. Product of two polynomials that are represented in point value form | IV. Θ(n lg n) |

List I to List II matching for FFT and polynomial algorithm running times

## Q3 - Options
(A) A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV
(B) A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
(C) A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
(D) A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q2

Each pairing depends on a distinct algorithmic complexity result.

A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

- Parallel FFT runs in Θ(lg n) time because the butterfly network of the FFT computation can be evaluated across O(lg n) parallel stages.
- Iterative FFT, the standard sequential divide-and-conquer FFT, runs in Θ(n lg n) time.
- Evaluating a degree n-1 polynomial at n points using Horner's method costs Θ(n) per point, so evaluating at all n points costs Θ(n²).
- Multiplying two polynomials already given in point-value form only needs a pointwise multiplication of the y-values, which is Θ(n).

## Q4
FFTs are \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ techniques used to encode digital video and audio information and helps analyse the signal in \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ domain.

## Q4 - Options
(A) Encryption, time
(B) Encryption, frequency
(C) Compression, time
(D) Compression, frequency

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q26

The Fast Fourier Transform converts a time-domain signal into its frequency-domain representation, which is the standard first step used in multimedia compression schemes for audio and video.

By concentrating a signal's energy into fewer significant frequency coefficients, FFT-based transforms let compression algorithms discard perceptually less important components, which is a compression technique, not an encryption one, and the analysis it performs happens in the frequency domain rather than the time domain.

## Q5
For matrix multiplication, if we use divide and conquer algorithm, then \_\_\_\_\_\_

A. the running time is T(n)=Θ(n³)<br>
B. the running time is T(n)= Θ(n² log n)<br>
C. The recurrence can be defined as T(n)=8T(n/2)+Θ(n²)<br>
D. the recurrence relation is T(n)= 8T(2n)+Θ(n²log n)<br>
E. Masters theorem, one of the cases is applicable

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

## Q5 - Options
(A) A, C, E only
(B) A, D, E only
(C) B, D, E only
(D) B, C, D only

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q57

Splitting each n×n matrix into four n/2×n/2 submatrices and combining their products directly (without Strassen's trick) requires 8 recursive multiplications plus Θ(n²) work for additions, giving the recurrence T(n) = 8T(n/2) + Θ(n²), which matches statement C.

Applying the Master theorem to this recurrence with a=8, b=2, so log_b(a) = log₂8 = 3, and since the Θ(n²) term grows polynomially slower than n³, this falls under the case where T(n) = Θ(n^log_b a) = Θ(n³), confirming statement A and showing the Master theorem is indeed applicable, confirming statement E.

Statement B's Θ(n² log n) does not match this recurrence's actual solution, and statement D's T(n)=8T(2n)+Θ(n²log n) is not a valid divide-and-conquer recurrence at all, since recursive subproblems must shrink, not grow.

Since A, C, and E all hold, the correct option is A, C, E only.

## Q6
Given the FFT we can have \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ time procedure for multiplying two polynomials A(x) and B(x) of degree bound n where input and output representations are in coefficient form, assuming n is a power of 2.

## Q6 - Options
(A) O(n²)
(B) O(n log₂ n)
(C) O(2ⁿ)
(D) O(log₂ n)

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q27

Direct coefficient-form multiplication needs O(n²) work, because every coefficient of A must be multiplied against every coefficient of B.

The FFT-based approach avoids this by converting both polynomials to point-value form using the FFT in O(n log n), multiplying the point-values pairwise in O(n), and converting the product back to coefficient form with an inverse FFT in O(n log n).

The two FFT steps dominate, so the overall procedure runs in O(n log₂ n) time, much faster than the naive O(n²) approach.

## Q7
Statement I: Given a graph G=(V,E) in which each vertex v in V has an associated positive weight w(v), we can use linear programming to find the lower bound on the weight of the minimum-weight vertex cover.

Statement II: The lower bound can be found by maximizing the objective Σ w(v)x(v) over all v in V, subject to x(u)+x(v) ≥ 1 for each edge (u,v) in E.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

## Q7 - Options
(A) Both statement I and Statement II are correct
(B) Both statement I and Statement II are incorrect
(C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
(D) Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct

## Q7 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q89

Linear programming relaxation is a standard technique for bounding weighted vertex cover, so Statement I correctly describes a real approach.

The standard LP relaxation for minimum weight vertex cover minimizes Σ w(v)x(v) subject to x(u)+x(v)≥1 for every edge, because minimizing a covering objective under a relaxed LP gives a lower bound on the true integer optimum.

Maximizing that same objective, as Statement II proposes, does not produce a lower bound on a minimization problem at all, so Statement II describes the wrong direction of optimization and is incorrect.

## Q8
Consider the following statements of approximation algorithm:<br>
Statement I: Vertex-cover is a polynomial time 2-approximation algorithm.<br>
Statement II: TSP-tour is a polynomial time 3-approximation algorithm for travelling salesman problem with the triangle inequality.<br>
Which of the following is correct?

## Q8 - Options
(A) Statement I true and Statement II false
(B) Statement I and Statement II true
(C) Statement I false and Statement II true
(D) Statement I and Statement II false

## Q8 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q77

Statement I is true. The standard vertex-cover approximation algorithm, which greedily picks both endpoints of an uncovered edge, runs in polynomial time and always returns a cover at most twice the size of the optimal one, a 2-approximation.

Statement II is false. For metric TSP, the well-known polynomial-time approximation guarantee is a 2-approximation using a minimum spanning tree, and Christofides' algorithm improves this to a 3/2-approximation. Neither of the standard results gives a 3-approximation, so Statement II's claimed ratio is incorrect.

## Q9
The time complexity to multiply two polynomials of degree n using Fast Fourier transform method is:

## Q9 - Options
(A) θ(n lg n)
(B) θ(n²)
(C) θ(n)
(D) θ(lg n)

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2019 (4 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q28

Multiplying two polynomials of degree n using the Fast Fourier Transform involves three stages:

1. Evaluation: compute the Discrete Fourier Transform of each polynomial at 2n points using FFT, taking θ(n lg n) time.
2. Pointwise multiplication: multiply the point-value representations in θ(n) time.
3. Interpolation: compute the Inverse FFT to obtain the product polynomial coefficients in θ(n lg n) time.

The overall asymptotic time complexity is θ(n lg n).

## Q10
The following multithreaded algorithm computes transpose of a matrix in parallel:

```
p Trans (X, Y, N)
if N = 1
 then Y[1,1] ← X[1,1]
else partition X into four (N/2) × (N/2) submatrices X₁₁, X₁₂, X₂₁, X₂₂
 partition Y into four (N/2) × (N/2) submatrices Y₁₁, Y₁₂, Y₂₁, Y₂₂
 spawn p Trans (X₁₁, Y₁₁, N/2)
 spawn p Trans (X₁₂, Y₂₁, N/2)
 spawn p Trans (X₂₁, Y₁₂, N/2)
 spawn p Trans (X₂₂, Y₂₂, N/2)
```

What is the asymptotic parallelism of the algorithm?

## Q10 - Options
(A) T₁/T∞ or θ(N²/lg N)
(B) T₁/T∞ or θ(N/lg N)
(C) T₁/T∞ or θ(lg N/N²)
(D) T₁/T∞ or θ(lg N/N)

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2019 (4 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q52

Analyzing work T₁ and span T∞ for the divide-and-conquer parallel transpose:

1. Work T₁(N) (serial running time):<br>
   T₁(N) = 4T₁(N/2) + θ(1)<br>
   By Master Theorem Case 1, N^(log₂ 4) = N², so T₁(N) = θ(N²).
2. Span T∞(N) (critical-path length with parallel spawns):<br>
   T∞(N) = T∞(N/2) + θ(1)<br>
   By Master Theorem Case 2, T∞(N) = θ(lg N).
3. Parallelism:<br>
   Parallelism = T₁ / T∞ = θ(N² / lg N).

## Q11
The second smallest of n elements can be found with \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ comparisons in the worst case.

## Q11 - Options
(A) 3n/2
(B) n + ceil(lg n) – 2
(C) lg n
(D) n–1

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Algorithms: Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, String Matching & More
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q45

Using a tournament tree algorithm, finding the second smallest element requires exactly n + ceil(lg n) - 2 comparisons in the worst case.

- Finding the minimum element among n elements using a knockout tournament takes n - 1 comparisons.
- The second smallest element can only have lost directly to the overall minimum during one of the tournament rounds.
- The height of the binary tournament tree is ceil(lg n), meaning the minimum element participated in at most ceil(lg n) comparisons.
- Finding the smallest element among these ceil(lg n) direct losers takes ceil(lg n) - 1 comparisons.
- Total worst-case comparisons = (n - 1) + (ceil(lg n) - 1) = n + ceil(lg n) - 2.
- Therefore, Option B is the exact bound.
